Sister app to Analysis Acrobat, which teaches you to analyse the language you find here.

Practise

No timer and no score anywhere in here, because this is where you get better rather than where you prove it. Pick what you want to work on, and keep going at it.

SOAPMAPS

Eight things writers do to make description work. You will not find all eight in one sentence, and you do not need to: the point is to notice which one is doing the work in front of you.

A sentence is often several of these at once. The icy wind whispered angrily at the window is adjectives, personification, adverbs, powerful verbs and senses all together, and whispered is two of them by itself. That is why the find-it rounds ask you to find a technique rather than to name one: the question is where it is doing its work. When the app does ask you to name one, the phrase has been chosen so that only one answer fits, and in Spot them all a phrase that is also a second technique is never marked wrong.

The harder techniques

Once SOAPMAPS is second nature, these come next. They turn up constantly in the texts you are given and rarely in the ones you write, which is the gap this set is here to close.

Words for talking about technique

Not techniques you find, but words you use when you write about them.

Three of these are about sound rather than picture. Alliteration is the family; plosive alliteration and sibilance are two of its members, named after the sounds doing the work. A run of s and sh at the start of words is both sibilance and alliteration, so if you are asked to find the alliteration you have not got it wrong by finding a hiss there.
Personification, anthropomorphism and zoomorphism. In SOAPMAPS, anything made to act like a human counts as personification. The harder techniques only ask a sharper question: which way round is the borrowing? Anthropomorphism gives a thing or an animal a person's thoughts and feelings; zoomorphism does the opposite and borrows from an animal, so a car that growls is zoomorphism.

How to spot each class

Always look at the word inside its sentence, never on its own. The same word can do different jobs: run is a verb in "I run every morning" and a noun in "I went for a run".

No check is perfect, which is why every card ends with its exceptions. If a check gives you an odd answer, that is usually the exception showing up, not your mistake.

                            Reference:

                            The techniques explained

                            These are eight language techniques you will meet most often in the texts you read: six from SOAPMAPS (adjectives and adverbs have their own place in Word classes), plus alliteration and hyperbole. For each one there is a clear definition, a few worked examples, and a note on how to write about it well. Remember: in the exam, naming a technique earns very little on its own. The marks come from explaining the effect it creates.

                            Simile

                            Comparison using like or as. The two things are different, but they share a quality the writer wants you to notice.

                            as cold as ice

                            Describes something freezing, or a person who is unfeeling and unwelcoming.

                            the crowd roared like a hungry beast

                            The noise is huge and threatening; the crowd seems wild and almost animal.

                            Going deeper: always ask what quality the comparison transfers. "Her smile was like sunshine" is not about light, it is about warmth and happiness.

                            Metaphor

                            Saying a thing is something else. There is no "like" or "as", which makes it a more direct, more daring comparison than a simile: it states that the two things are one.

                            the classroom was a zoo

                            Noisy, chaotic and out of control, full of wild behaviour.

                            he was drowning in paperwork

                            Overwhelmed and unable to cope, sinking under the sheer amount.

                            Going deeper: because a metaphor insists the two things are the same, it often feels stronger and more certain than a simile.

                            Personification

                            Making things act like humans. The thing is given human qualities, feelings or actions: an object, the weather, or an idea. (The harder techniques add two sharper names: anthropomorphism, where a thing or an animal is given a person's own thoughts and feelings, and zoomorphism, the opposite move, which borrows from an animal instead of a person.)

                            the wind whispered through the trees

                            Whispering is human, so the wind seems gentle, secretive and almost alive.

                            fear gripped her heart

                            Fear is treated like a person seizing her, making it feel powerful and physical.

                            Going deeper: personification is a special kind of metaphor: a metaphor that gives specifically human qualities to a non-human thing. Every personification is a metaphor, but not every metaphor is personification. Because "personification" is the more precise label, use it whenever the human quality is clear.

                            How comparisons work: tenor and vehicle

                            Simile, metaphor and personification all work in the same way: they describe one thing by comparing it to another. The thing being described is the tenor; the thing it is compared to is the vehicle. The vehicle lends, or bestows, its qualities onto the tenor.

                            as cold as ice

                            The tenor is the person being described; the vehicle is ice. Ice is cold, hard and unfeeling, so those qualities are passed to the tenor.

                            To analyse a comparison well, name the vehicle and ask: what qualities does it carry, and which of them are being transferred to the tenor? "Her words were daggers" works because daggers are sharp, sudden and wounding, and that pain is given to her words. Spotting the vehicle and its qualities is the fastest route to a strong Move 2. You can drill exactly this in .

                            Powerful verb

                            Words for exciting actions. A strong, vivid verb chosen for its energy or precision, used instead of a plain, ordinary one.

                            she sprinted to the door

                            Far more urgent than "ran": it suggests speed, panic or desperation.

                            he devoured his dinner

                            More than "ate": greedy, fast, an almost animal hunger.

                            Going deeper: a powerful verb can be another technique at the same time. If it gives a human action to a non-human thing it is also personification ("the storm raged"); if it imitates a sound it is also onomatopoeia ("the gate slammed").

                            Senses

                            Words that appeal to what we see, hear, smell, taste or touch. They build a vivid picture or atmosphere.

                            the velvety darkness

                            Appeals to touch: the dark feels soft, rich, almost comforting.

                            a bitter wind

                            Appeals to taste and touch: the wind is harsh, unpleasant, even painful.

                            Going deeper: always say which sense the word appeals to, and the mood it creates.

                            Onomatopoeia

                            Words that make sounds. The word imitates the noise it describes, so the reader almost hears the scene.

                            the bacon sizzled

                            You can almost hear the spitting, hissing fat.

                            the gate clanged shut

                            A hard, metallic, final sound that suggests being trapped or shut out.

                            Going deeper: many onomatopoeic words are also powerful verbs (sizzle, clang, rustle). The effect is that the reader hears the moment, not just pictures it.

                            Alliteration

                            The same sound starting words close together.

                            the wild and windy weather

                            The repeated "w" adds force and rhythm, almost like gusts of wind.

                            slippery, slithering snake

                            The soft "s" sounds imitate the snake's hiss and gliding movement.

                            Going deeper: alliteration is about sound, not spelling. Its effect is often to draw attention to a phrase or to echo the thing described: soft sounds for softness, harsh sounds for harshness.

                            Hyperbole

                            Exaggeration so large it is not meant to be believed.

                            a mountain of homework

                            The amount feels impossibly large and overwhelming.

                            I have told you a thousand times

                            Exaggerates to show deep frustration at having to repeat something.

                            Going deeper: hyperbole always reveals a strong feeling, such as frustration, exhaustion or awe. Explain the feeling it exaggerates.

                            One phrase, more than one technique

                            Techniques often overlap. "The storm howled" is a powerful verb, onomatopoeia and personification all at once. When this happens in the exam, you do not have to name them all: choose the one technique whose effect you can explain best, and write about that in depth.

                              What to practise

                              Said or suggested: the difference (tap to read)

                              Every strong analysis makes two moves about a quotation.

                              Move 1: explicit (literal) meaning. What the words actually say or do. The plain, surface meaning you could point to.

                              Move 2: implied (deeper) meaning. What the words suggest, hint at, or make the reader feel: the associations a word carries and its effect on the reader. This is where the higher marks are won.

                              his words were ice

                              Explicit: he spoke in a cold, unfriendly way.

                              Implied: he wants to push others away and refuses any warmth or closeness.

                              The most common mistake is a Move 2 that only rewords Move 1. "His tone was chilly and unwelcoming" is still the literal meaning in new words.

                              The test: if your Move 2 could swap places with Move 1 without losing anything, it is only a reworded Move 1.

                                Reference:

                                Better than shows

                                The writer shows is never wrong, but it claims almost nothing. Each word here claims something more exact, and that is the point: celebrates and criticises take opposite sides, and exposes says something was hidden and usually bad. So choose the word that is true of the text, never just the fanciest one. Swapping shows for exposes everywhere is the bolted-on writing examiners notice.
